newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Public TV not exempt from EU rules, Van Miert says.
newsitem.headline: Public TV not exempt from EU rules, Van Miert says.

text.p: Public television is not free from European Union competition rules despite an agreement by EU leaders in Amsterdam, European Competition chief Karel Van Miert said on Thursday.

The agreement allows national governments to fund public service obligations, for example to help a TV channel devote resources to news, cultural and religious programmes. It was greeted by public broadcasters as a major victory.
Van Miert said it was legitimate to compensate public TV channels for such obligations, but the Commission would be carefully watching for any disguised subsidies.

"It is out of the question that they should be over-compensated or the Commission would be able to act," he told reporters at a briefing on a Commission decision to order Belgium to scrap an advertising monopoly granted to TV channel VTM.

The agreement, a protocol attached to a new EU treaty thrashed out at the Amsterdam summit of EU heads of government last week, asserts member states' right to provide for the funding of public service broadcasting in so far as such funding is granted for the fulfilment of the public service.
It also says that such funding must not affect trading conditions and competition in the EU to an extent which would be contrary to the common interest.
Commercial television fiercely opposed the attempt, originated by Belgium, to exempt their public rivals from EU competition rules.
They have also increasingly complained to the Commission about the financing of public channels arguing that state subsidies are often used to slash advertising prices.
A study commissioned by the EU executive shows that many public broadcasters are funded by licence fee and/or state money as well as advertising revenue.
